title.en: The Stars Are Coals and Ashes

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 14

summary.en: The Moon lets moonwater fall so 'Kaggen's new shoes stay wet and unwearable; when the Sun burns them by his fire, the Owl — the Mantis's other daughter — flings the coals and glowing ash into the sky, crying 'Coals, become Stars! Ash, become the Milky Way!' A whirlwind carries them above the clouds. The Sun curses her: by day she is blind and mocked; by night she flies among her stars — and evil-doers multiply.
summary.zh: 月降月水，令螳螂新鞋常濕不可穿；日以其火焚之。梟——螳螂之另一女——擲炭與熾灰上天，呼「炭化為星！灰化為銀河！」旋風舉之過雲。日咒其晝盲受嘲；夜則翔於己星之間——而惡行者自此滋長。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
The Moon came out of the right-foot shoe of the 'Hotnotsgod 'Kaggen. He made himself another pair of shoes in place of it. But the Moon did not like it that 'Kaggen should tramp on his masters, the shoes, by walking in them; so she let moonwater fall to keep the shoes wet, so that 'Kaggen could never put them on.

The 'Hotnotsgod called his other daughter, she who later became the Owl, and told her to place the wet shoes beside the Fire to dry. This again the Sun did not like, that 'Kaggen should dare put his dirty shoes beside the Fire; so he made the fire flame fiercely, so that the shoes were burnt. When the 'Hotnotsgod sent for his shoes they were burnt, and he scolded the Owl not a little.

The Owl herself was angered by it, and she took the coals and threw them into the sky, crying out: 'Come, coals, become Stars, that we may have light by night when the Moon and Sun sleep!' And to the glowing ashes she said: 'Come, ashes, become the Milky Way, to help the Stars give light. Give light, that the people may see by night and need not sit at home.' Then a great whirlwind came and carried the coals and ashes high above the clouds: the glittering coals became the flickering Stars, and the glowing ash became the Milky Way, which stands like a lit arch over the earth. Then there was light enough to walk by night.

When the Sun rose next day behind the mountains he saw the Owl sitting and asked her: 'Who has filled the sky with coals and ashes?' The Owl answered: 'I; for it is so dark by night that no one can see to walk.' Then the Sun said: 'Do you know that you have done a great evil? Now the people will walk about by night to do evil. I made the nights so dark that people could not see their hands before their eyes, and then they had to stay at home and sleep — the day is long enough to hunt and go about, to talk and make merry; but now you have opened the door for evil. I shall strive hard to get the Moon out of the sky, so that no moonshine comes; by day I shall wipe the Stars away before me. But as for you, my sister: henceforth you shall fly about by night with starlight; for if I see you by day I shall burn you to ashes as I did the shoes. Everyone who sees you will mock you for that foolish deed. Go, out of my sight, and prowling in the night! And you shall find that the Stars will give you sadly little light — just enough for evildoers to do evil. The Stars are too small to give you warmth; so by night you will sit shivering and shaking with cold.'

The Owl flew away to hide herself; for wherever she flies by day she is mocked. And now she sits pondering what she has done — whether it was right or wrong. Where she sits she calls out 'Ho, hoa' — which in the Bushman tongue means 'uplift, uplifted' — asking herself whether she did evil by throwing the coals and ashes up into the sky or lifting them up. The Sun blinded the Owl by day; so from that day she never saw her brother the Sun again. She delights now in the Stars and the Milky Way, or Heaven-road, which she herself made. And so it came about, as the Sun foretold: from then on lion, leopard, wolf, jackal and aardvark prowl again by night to murder and rob; from then on the evildoers multiplied, for they had now light enough by night to see, while others could not make them out from afar.

functions: Origin of the stars and Milky Way as flung coals and ashes.
Explains the owl's day-blindness and its 'ho-ho' cry as self-questioning.
Explains night crime as the consequence of opening the dark to light.

variants.name: |Xam girl-made-stars (Specimens)
variants.summary: The |Xam tell instead of a seclusion girl who threw wood-ashes and roots into the sky to make the Milky Way and the stars.

variants.name: Owl as star-reader (Deel I No. 16)
variants.summary: The Owl reads every person's star; comets and falling stars carry tidings of death.

title.en: The Hammerkop and the Frogs: Flowers and Naughty Children
title.zh: 鎚頭鸛與蛙：水花與頑童

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 15

summary.en: The Hammerkop, once a daughter of the Mantis, sees all things in the water and tells them truly; girls who foul the springs are slain by thunder-stones and become the water's flowers, and disobedient children who wade in become frogs that sing and dance for the Water-Snake by night. Children who kill frogs with stones are carried into the clouds by the whirlwind and rained down as frogs.
summary.zh: 鎚頭鸛本為螳螂之女，於水中見萬象而誠言之；污泉之少女遭雷石擊斃，化為水中之花；違命戲水之童化為蛙，夜為水蛇歌舞。擊蛙之童被旋風捲入雲中，隨雨降為蛙。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 15 (1919); not verbatim. The Hammerkop is not just today's bird: she was first a person of the old race and is a daughter of the 'Hotnotsgod, who changed her into a bird. She is well befriended with the Waters, who show her the portraits of everything that happens and still shall happen; she sees in the water things happening far away and understands their meaning.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 15; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Waters are holy to her. If the young girls foul them, let wood-ash fall into a fountain, or spill a pot of water into the fire, she tells it to the great Water-Snake and to Danser the Fire-man; these raise clouds and throw out fiery thunder-stones to kill the girls. Where they lie dead the streams wash them to a pool of water, and there they become flowers that grow in the Waters — therefore mothers still warn their children never to pick the Waters' flowers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 15; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. If children are naughty and walk into the water, the flowers dive under, the great Water-Snake pulls the disobedient ones under, and they become frogs, to sing and dance for the great Water-Snake by night. Once children stoned the frogs to death at the water; the Wind caught the naughty children in a whirlwind, carried them into the clouds, changed them into frogs, and it rained frogs out of the sky; then it changed the parents into frogs too, as a punishment for disobedience.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 15; not verbatim.

title.en: The Owl and the Mice: The Liar's Punishment

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 16

summary.en: The Owl reads every person's own star; a flashing star means a friend's death, and spirits ride the moon's hollow bowl. Two lying old people pelt her, steal her knife and hide her under the karosses; a lion sent to tear them in the night; the moonwater falls on the shreds of their flesh and each piece becomes a Mouse. So mice are born of liars, thieves and deceivers.
summary.zh: 梟讀每人之星；星閃即有亡者，靈乘月之空匙。二老謊者擲石、竊刀、覆之於皮褥下；獅夜裂其身；月水落其碎肉，每片化為鼠。故鼠乃謊者、竊賊、欺詐者之後裔。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 16 (1919); not verbatim. Every person has his own Star. If a star shines especially bright, or flashes, or gets a tail, the Owl knows at once whose star it is and where she must carry the tidings. The Stars also talk with her by sending messages with the fireflies; and the Moon tells her much, for the Moon can see far over the world. When the hollow bowl of the Moon fills up, the spirits give way; at Full Moon there is no place for them — it is climbing-out time.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 16; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Owl told two old people, an old bachelor and an old maid, that they must flee at once, for a lion was seeking them to eat them. They called her a liar, dropped her knife when she let it fall, refused to give it back, thrust her under the karosses and scolded her with ugly words; and the Owl flew away grieved. In the night it rained hard; the lion's roar came nearer; they fled, were handed skins at another fire, but were given up to the lion when the Owl told who they were, and the lion tore them to pieces without licking blood or eating flesh.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 16; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In the night the moonwater fell on the pieces of flesh, life came into them, and every piece became a Mouse. So the Mice sprang from liars, thieves and deceivers, and therefore they cannot leave off their tricks to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 16; not verbatim.

title.en: The Rainbow, Daughter of the Mirage

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 17

summary.en: The rainbow, wordless daughter of the Mirage, loved fine clothes and had two suitors: the Wind-bird, scented with all sweet flowers, and the Rain-Beast. The Wind-bird carries her to his cold cliff-house and returns to fetch food; she slips home and hides underground. The Rain-Beast, lulled by buchu she strews on him, sleeps under a tree and wakes believing she still sits on his back — so the Mirage changed her daughter into a Rainbow, that Wind and Rain may see and admire her but do her no harm.
summary.zh: 虹——蜃景之啞女——愛美服，有二求者：體裹百花之香的風鳥，與雨獸。風鳥攜其至寒崖之家，返取食；她潛歸匿於地下。雨獸被她所撒布庫草催眠，睡於樹下，醒時猶以為她在其背。蜃景遂化其女為虹——使風雨可見可慕而無害。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 17 (1919); not verbatim. The Rainbow is the daughter of the Mirage. Like her mother she took great pleasure in making fun of someone, and therefore she was so fond of putting on beautiful clothes. She had many suitors, among them the Wind-bird and the Rain-Beast; but the Wind is stronger than the Rain, so she had to await her turn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 17; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Wind-bird flew to her scented with the scents of all the sweet-smelling flowers, and she sat lovingly on his back as he flew with her to the mountains where his house was in a rock cave. But the cold air and the narrowness did not please her; while he flew far to fetch food she slipped home and hid herself underground with her mother, where the Wind-bird could never sniff her out.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 17; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Water-Snake, who also sails under the ground, soon found where the girl was hiding and told her father, the Rain-Beast. He came straight to her; she smelled the sweet scent of the rain he makes, came up from her underground dwelling, and played with him, strewing finely pounded buchu over him until he fell asleep under a tree. Then she dropped away to her mother. When the Rain-Beast woke he imagined the girl still sat on his back, and walked on to his hippo-hole — and only in the water discovered she was gone. The Mirage burned rain-bushes to soothe him, and changed her daughter into a Rainbow, with her beautiful coloured clothes, so that the Wind and the Rain can see and admire her but do her no harm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 17; not verbatim.

title.en: 'Kaggen's Son Stoned: The Eye Played as a Ball (Afrikaans Version)
title.zh: 螳螂之子遭石擊：眼球為球（非洲語版）

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 18

summary.en: Sent to cut sticks for bows against the bobbejaans, 'Kaggen's son is mobbed; they break his skull, roll out his eye and play ball with it, crying 'It is my ball!' The Hammerkop tells 'Kaggen, who hides his tears, joins the game, and palms the eye into his knapsack. At the water he lays it in the pool crying 'Body of my son, come here!' — the body falls into the water beside the eye, and the boy, weak but alive, is brought home.
summary.zh: 螳螂遣子伐木製弓以擊狒狒；狒狒圍擊之，破其顱，滾出其眼，以為球戲，呼「此吾球也！」。鎚頭鸛報於螳螂；他拭淚入局，掌納眼於行囊。至水邊，置眼於池，呼「吾子之軀，來此！」——軀自空而落，與眼同池；子弱而復生。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record. This is the Afrikaans-corpus variant of the |Xam baboons-and-eye myth.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 18 (1919); not verbatim. 'Kaggen sent his son to fetch sticks, of which he would make kieries and a bow to throw and shoot the people who sat on their heels. In the field the bobbejaans met the son; each called his mate to come and listen to the boy's words, until even the old leader came; and the old one cried: 'Who else is meant but us! Seize the boy, take the sticks from him and beat him!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 18; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The crowd of bobbejaans fell upon the boy and beat him with sticks and fists till his skull broke and his eye rolled out of his head; the boy was dead. One grabbed the eye and cried: 'Here is a fine thing to play ball with!' They stood in a ring; whoever caught the eye cried 'It is my ball!', threw it on, and they tumbled over one another till the dust rose.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 18; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Hammerkop, who sees everything, flew to the 'Hotnotsgod to tell what the bobbejaans had done to his son. 'Kaggen sprang up, took his bow, quiver and knapsack, and ran to the place; from afar he saw the dust as the bobbejaans played ball. He dried the tears from his eyes so they should not see he had wept, laid down his weapons, and asked to play too; he caught the eye, and when he threw it, the eye flew up into the air and vanished. The bobbejaans searched his quiver and knapsack and found nothing; then they fell upon him with their fists, and the fight grew fierce; being many, they got the mastery, and 'Kaggen ran away with his things.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 18; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. By the water he took the eye out of his knapsack and laid it in the pool with the words: 'Come, body of my son, come here; lie here in the water, that your eye may grow again on its place, and become as you were before.' Then the body of the son came through the air and fell into the water beside the eye. 'Kaggen went home sick of the beating; later he returned with a front-skin and kaross, caught the boy as he tried to spring into the water, and said: 'Do not be afraid; I am your father 'Kaggen... The waters have raised him again out of the dead; he is still weak, and we must all care for him till he is strong and fresh again.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 18; not verbatim.

title.en: The Maid of the Waters and Her Brother's Theft

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 19

summary.en: A girl cannot resist the flowers of the deep pool; stepping in, the Water-Snake draws her under — but she keeps her human shape and becomes the Maid of the Waters, drawing in whomever she will. Her brother tries to steal the snake's stone to free her; the snake meets him first and turns him into an old toad, his bow into a brittle stick, his arrows into chaff — and dries up every fountain to punish his parents, till the Maid in pity lets them draw water.
summary.zh: 少女難耐深池之花；入水即被蛇曳下——然保其人形，成為水女，能以無形之力曳人入水。其兄欲竊蛇石以救妹；蛇先發制人，化之為老蟾，化其弓為脆杖、其箭為穅——並令諸泉盡涸以懲其親；水女憐之，許其父母取水。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 19 (1919); not verbatim. There was a girl who always fetched water at a fountain, near which lay a great pool in which beautiful flowers grew. Her mother always warned her not to pick those beautiful flowers, for they were girls who had been carried off into the water to become flowers. But the flowers were too attractive, and the temptation too great; she stepped into the pool, the flowers vanished under the water, and the great Water-Snake at once drew the girl in after them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 19; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The girl did not become a flower or a frog; she remained a person, but gained the power to draw people into the water with her unseen will. So she wandered from one pool to another, and became the Maid of the Waters: in the water she has the power to draw people in invisibly, and outside she bewitches them with her beauty so that they follow her unbidden.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 19; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Her brother resolved to free his sister from the great Water-Snake by stealing the shining stone on her head, for without it the snake is powerless. His parents warned him in vain that if the snake were powerless all the fountains would dry of themselves. He went to spy out where she hid the stone; but the snake discovered his plan and stormed him before he had the stone in his hand: she changed him into an old common toad that lives far from the water, changed his bow into an old brittle stick, his quiver fell to pieces and the arrows in it withered to chaff; and she punished his parents by drying up all the fountains — until the Maid of the Waters, feeling for her parents, allowed them to draw water at the hippo-pool without drawing them in.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 19; not verbatim.

title.en: The Tortoise Witch and the Moon-Healed Hands

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 20

summary.en: A witch of the old race, mostly in the shape of a great tortoise, feigns neck-pain; each man who rubs her with fat is snapped into her shell, and tears his hands bloody freeing them. Their flesh and skin grow back as the moon waxes, from the moon-dew. They later trap her on her back with stones and send bewitched crows to pick her flesh — but she feels no pain, and her hollow shell breeds bees that sting the men nearly to death.
summary.zh: 古族之巫常化大龜，詐稱頸痛；凡以脂膏擦其頸者，皆被其首縮入殼中夾住，掙脫時手肉盡剝。月漸盈，其手肉隨月水漸復。後二人翻其仰臥壓之以石，遣被巫之鴉啄其肉——她卻不覺痛；其空殼招蜂群螫人幾斃。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic injury; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 20 (1919); not verbatim. In the days of the old race there was a witch who took great pleasure in hurting people. She took various shapes, but showed herself mostly in the shape of a great Tortoise... To carry out her tricks better she always played sick, so that people pitied her; and when they came to doctor her, they sat on the pin.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 20; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. 'My dear old brother, come near! I have such unbearable pain in my neck — rub my neck in with fat.' As the man rubbed, the tortoise snapped her neck into the shell, and his hand was fast. He tore it free with a stone, but all the flesh and skin came off — only bare sinews and bones remained. A second man suffered the same; and when the two came home the Moon was still young. Morning after morning they washed their hands with the dew, the water of the Moon; and as the Moon grew, the flesh grew over their bare sinews and bones, until at full moon their hands were perfectly healed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 20; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. They found her again on another spot, rolled her on her back and packed stones round her so she could not right herself; then they bewitched two Crows, so that where the witch's body was they must pick her flesh out of her shell alive. But the witch felt no pain and let the crows have their way; and as the men had bewitched the crows, so the old witch bewitched the Bees to sting people wherever they found them: when one man took up the empty shell, the bees swarmed out and stung him till he fell senseless on the road, throwing dust into the air to signal his distress.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 20; not verbatim.

title.en: The Morning Star Is the Heart of Dageraad

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 21

summary.en: Dageraad, eldest son of the murdered Sun, dims the little stars each morning and hangs the blue sky. Wolf's daughter, jealously spurned by his baby, drugs his wife's oribi-rice with her own shoulder-sweat; the wife's beads and kaross fall off, she becomes a tearing lioness, feeds her baby at the reeds, and is caught and flayed — keeping the ear-tufts, and becoming the rooikat that eats flesh, not ants. Wolf kills Dageraad at night; his shining heart flies up and becomes the Morning Star, and his children become the brightest stars that follow their parents.
summary.zh: 曙光——被弒太陽之長子——每晨暗淡小星、懸掛青天。狼女因嬰兒拒己而妒，以己肩汗下毒於其妻之蟻卵飯；妻珠飾衣裘盡落，化為裂獸母獅，於蘆叢哺嬰；被擒剝皮——留耳尖毛，成為食肉不食蟻之獰貓。狼夜殺曙光；其燦心飛升為晨星，其子女化為最亮之星，隨其父母而行。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains domestic poisoning and killing; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 21 (1919); not verbatim. The Sun was first a man of the old race, who walked with the light of his shining face; but the other old people grew wickedly angry at him and murdered him, and his children threw his shining head into the sky, where it shines to this day. The eldest son of the old man was very fond of his father, and became his messenger: his name was Dageraad (Daybreak).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 21; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. His first work early in the morning was to dim the lights of the little stars, and then to hang out the blue sky, behind which the little stars remain hidden; after that the Sun rises from his bed, and the son's work for the day is done. Wolf's daughter was madly in love with the handsome Dageraad; when his wife's baby refused to play with her she went weeping to her father, who advised her to throw the blackish sweat behind her shoulder-blades on the oribi-rice his wife would eat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 21; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Unmarked she threw her arm-sweat on the washed rice; when the wife ate it she felt herself going mad, her neck-rings and armbands fell off, her kaross and skin dress fell off, and all lay on the ground; Wolf's daughter picked them up and dressed herself in them. The wife felt she was becoming a wild animal and fled into the veld, hiding in a bed of reeds; three times a day her younger sister brought the baby to the reeds to be fed. Dageraad discovered the deceit at the evening dance, threw his assegai at the impostor, and burned her hind-foot in the fire as she fled.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 21; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The people drove bucks before them to the reed-bed; the lioness-wife was caught while she seized a buck, and her skin was pulled off — but she cried that the hair on the tips of her ears must be left, else she would go deaf; so she kept the tufts, and soon became the great Rooikat, which eats only flesh and no oribi-ants. Wolf boiled with rage at the treatment of his daughter, went by night to Dageraad's sleeping place, murdered him and began to skin him; but as he cut the body open the shining Heart flew out of it and rose into the air, and became from then on the great Morning Star; and all his family and descendants became stars that follow their parents and are now the brightest stars in the sky.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 21; not verbatim.

title.en: The Evening Star Is the Eye of Aandskemering

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1881 at Zoovoorbij on the Hantam River by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 22

summary.en: The two sons of the Sun, Daybreak and Evening-gleam, never got on. Wolf's widow drugs the pot of Evening-gleam's wife; the wife wakes muddled, loses her child and slowly becomes an Owl, weeping 'how-hoo' for it. Wolf's daughter returns the child, and Evening-gleam, for the child's sake, takes her — until the Hammerkop tells all. He pursues her to Wolf's house; Wolf leads him to the cliff-edge and pushes him into the gorge: one bright eye bursts, the other flies up and becomes the Evening Star; the child becomes the aardvark that comes out at dusk.
summary.zh: 日之二子——曙光與暮光——素不相睦。狼之寡女下毒於暮光妻之炊鍋；妻醒而昏亂，失其子，漸化為梟，夜夜「霍霍」哭子。狼女攜子而返；暮光為子而納她——直至鎚頭鸛揭其姦。他追至狼家；狼引其至崖邊，推之墜谷：一目迸裂，另一目飛升為昏星；其子化為黃昏出穴之土豚。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 22 (1919); not verbatim. The two sons of the Sun, Dageraad and Aandskemering, could not get on with each other from their young days. Dageraad's work lasted from daybreak to sunset, and he had not such good eyes, so he usually went to bed early; but Aandskemering had two great eyes that blazed like two flames of fire in the dark. His work began at sunset and lasted till dark; then he rattled about at night, or hunted and sought food.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 22; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The brothers quarrelled as they met at the first light of daybreak; each seized sand or water to throw, and each missed; Dageraad cried that his sand and dust would become mosquitoes and gnats to bite Aandskemering evening and night, and Aandskemering cried that his water would become the dew to wet Dageraad's path every morning. Wolf's widow, once more in love, asked her mother's advice, stole Aandskemering's child after drugging the pot, and the childless wife woke muddled, lost her memory, and slowly changed into an Owl, which wakes as her husband makes twilight and flies out to kill mice and weep for her child.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 22; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf's daughter came back with the child on her back, and for the child's sake, which called him pa-pa, Aandskemering took her as wife. But at dusk came a Hammerkop flying, which sees everything in the water, and it called for the Owl; the whole deceit was told. Wolf's daughter seized the child and fled on her back; Aandskemering pursued her to Wolf's house, and Wolf, after much arguing, said: 'Come walk with me to that rock cliff, and I will show you that your wife and child sit there fresh and healthy, waiting for you.' When they stood on the brink of the abyss, Wolf pushed Aandskemering down into the gorge. One of his bright eyes burst on the spot, but the other flew up into the sky and became the great shining Evening Star. The child grieved till it became the Aardvark, which comes out when it grows dusk and sees to be home in the rock-crack before daybreak. And the Owl still sits and weeps for her child, while Wolf still pushes Aandskemering behind the western ridge into the abyss every evening.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 22; not verbatim.

title.en: Dampertjie and Spuitertjie Shoot with Lightning
title.zh: 丹普與斯普伊特以雷電相射

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 23

summary.en: The witness of the Sun's murder dare not speak; he confides the secret into a stopped-up aardvark hole, gemsbok hoofprints open it, and the rotten words rise as a blue-black mist. The liver-bird sings the secret to the Sun; the old sorcerer changes the man into Dampertjie — the blue-black bug whose touch squirts a mist — and Wolkop into Spuitertjie, whose arrows became water that burns like fire. White lightning strikes without noise and does not kill; black lightning kills without noise.
summary.zh: 日之弒案目擊者不敢言；將祕密吐入封閉之土豚穴；大羚蹄踏開穴口，腐語化為青黑之霧。肝雀唱其祕於日；老巫化其為丹普——觸之噴霧之青黑小蟲；化沃克普為斯普伊特，其箭化為如火之水。白雷轟鳴而不殺；黑雷無聲而致命。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 23 (1919); not verbatim. When the Sun was still a man of the old race his mates murdered him; another man, sitting on an anthill nearby, saw the whole murder, and saw that Wolkop (Cloud-head) was the leader of the murderers, and saw how Wolkop's wife and other maids sent their children to throw the head of the Sun into the air. Wolkop threatened to cut him in living strips of flesh if he ever told.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 23; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The secret gnawed him, but he dared not open his mouth; so he stopped up an aardvark hole, leaving only a little opening, and spoke into it: 'It is Wolkop, the scoundrel; It is Wolkop and his mates; Also Wolkop's children, Who do evil and keep still — It is they! ... The Sunman They tortured — It is they!' and he stopped the hole tight before the words could escape. Then he could eat and laugh freely again. Gemsbok ran over the hole and one hoof broke it open, and a blue-black mist came out of the trample-hole: the words, gone rotten, were that mist. A liver-bird (lewerkie) heard from those words who had led the murderers of the old man, the Sun, and still sings the message to the Sun every morning in glad song.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 23; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The old sorcerer, brother of the Sun, changed the silent man into a Dampertjie, the blue-black little bug that squirts a mist from its body when touched, walking on the sand the Sun has scorched. He changed Wolkop into the Spuitertjie-bug, whose arrows became water that burns like fire; and Spuitertjie stole Dampertjie's sister and her bag of burning water. Dampertjie shot black lightning from his black clouds at the white clouds of Spuitertjie, who shot flashing white lightning; a black bolt struck Spuitertjie down, and his kicking on the ground is the rumbling of the thunder. The Bushmen say: black lightning makes no noise and kills; white lightning makes a noise but does not kill.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 23; not verbatim.

title.en: The Animals Ask for Food and Water

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 24

summary.en: When animals and people were made they had no food or water, so each ate the other's flesh. The great Elephant volunteered to die: his bones shall become fruit-trees, his sinews climbing plants with watermelons, his hair the grass. The great Water-Snake alone is strong enough to kill him, bites him dead, and later burrows underground to make the subterranean waters; the moon and stars weep with the thirsty plants and their tears fall as dew; and a grass-loving Beast flings fountain-water into the sky to make the first rain.
summary.zh: 獸與人初造時無食無水，遂相食。大象自請死：其骨化果樹，其筋化藤蔓結瓜，其毛化草。唯大水蛇力足以殺之，噬而斃之，後鑿地成地下水；月星與渴者草木同泣，淚為晨露；喜草之巨獸舀泉水上天，降下初雨。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
When the Animals and also the People were made, they had no food and no water. So one animal had to eat the flesh of another and drink its blood; this gave rise to wailing among them, but what else could they do? They wept over their condition and sought improvement.

A very great Elephant, so big that he could see over a ridge or hill, spoke and said: 'When I am dead, I shall have it much better than now. Then I am a great Spirit, which needs no food and no water; for Spirits do not eat and drink; and when I am a Spirit, I shall provide for you all. My bones I shall let become trees, which can bear fruit for you; my sinews shall become plants that creep on the ground and bear watery melons and wild cucumbers for you; and my hair shall grow on the ground and become grass. Then you shall have food more than enough.' The Animals asked: 'How long are you going to live yet? And how long must we wait? For an Elephant becomes very old.' He answered: 'How long I shall live, I do not know. All you have to do is to await your time.'

The Animals asked: 'Where do we get water to drink?' Then the great old Snake, with the shining stone on its head, gave answer: 'So eager to die am I not; but I shall think over a plan to make water. When I am dead I cannot do it.' Of all the Animals strong enough to kill the great Elephant, the great Snake with the shining stone on its head was the only one — it was not only very strong, but also very venomous. That great Snake called out: 'Great Elephant, you have spoken your own sentence. You must keep your word! On this spot you must die, then you and we shall all be happier than now.' Thereupon the great Snake attacked the great Elephant and bit him dead with its venom. Then all the Animals had at first enough food and drink in the flesh and blood of the Elephant.

That same evening the Animals saw the great Spirit of the Elephant, with two great fiery eyes and mouth, walking about; but the Spirit walked away and did nothing for them. So he came evening after evening to look at his carrion, on which the Animals ate until nothing remained but bones, sinews and hair. Then the Spirit spoke to the bones, the sinews and the hair, that they must become trees, climbing plants and grass, which must provide food for the Animals, and that they must bear their own seeds, to propagate themselves further. Then trees, climbing plants and grass came.

But there was still no water. For this the great Snake had promised to care. So the Animals spoke to the great Snake and asked why he still delayed to make water. On the spot he crawled under the ground and made the underground waters, which stand in fountains or bubble up. The grass and trees by the fountain-places grew lush and luxuriant; but the plants on the mountains and plains pined, withered and dried up. Then those plants wept and begged the little Stars and the Moon to pour their water by night over the trees, climbing plants and grass. But the Moon and Stars answered that they had only enough water for their own use, and could not spare any of it. So the plants that grew on mountains and plains wept. The plants by the water-sources wept with them over the fate of their brothers and sisters. This mourning wailing was too much for the Moon and the Stars, who also wept bitterly with the thirsty ones; and their tears fell by night in drops on the leaves of the plants, so that in the morning they are wet with dew.

There was a great Beast that was very fond of eating grass, and could never get enough of it. He said he would make rain to pour out everywhere over the fields. He took of the waters of the fountains and threw it into the sky. He walked from fountain to fountain and flung water into the air. The winds came from afar and drove all that water high into the sky together, so that clouds formed; then he carried the clouds, which shook out rain, over the fields; and so the first rains came. Later, when drought comes over the land, that Rain-Beast is led about to show him the places that are dry; the places not shown to him stay dry until one day they go and show him those places. From then on there was enough food and water for all the Animals. But some Animals were too murderous and defiant, and would not stop killing and devouring: lion, leopard, wolf, the wild cats, falcon, owl and many others wanted nothing but flesh. The Vulture said he was content with the carrion of dead Animals. And so the world still exists today: the one lives off the other, and without the other the one cannot exist.

functions: Creation charter: food plants and grass from the dismembered Elephant.
Origin of subterranean waters and dew as collaborative creation.
Explains predation and carrion-feeding as part of the ordered world.

variants.name: Dismembered-primordial-being parallels
variants.summary: Like Ymir (Norse), Pangu (Chinese) and Purusha (Hindu), the Elephant's body becomes the world's vegetation.

Then you shall have food more than enough.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 24; not verbatim.

That evening the Animals saw the great Spirit of the Elephant, with two fiery eyes and mouth, walking about, doing nothing for them; and the Spirit spoke to the bones, sinews and hair that they must become trees, climbing plants and grass, bearing their own seeds — and so they came.

title.en: The Bushman's Prayers: Sun, Moon, Stars, Snake and Rain-Beast
title.zh: 桑人之祈禱：日月星蛇雨獸

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 25

summary.en: After a cold hungry night the Bushman turns his covered face to the rising Sun and prays: 'Make me as strong as you... throw me that worn-out food you do not need... hold my arm when I shoot at game.' To the new moon he cries: 'Take my old face from me, give me your new face... save me from the punishment the Hare brought on us.' To the stars: 'Take my heart that lacks; give me your heart that beats in plenty... take my arm, which shoots so badly.' And to the Water-Snake: 'Give us water in the desert... stop up the fountains when you hear the tramp of strangers.'
summary.zh: 寒飢之夜後，桑人掩目向初升之日祈曰：「使我如爾之強……擲爾不需之餘食予我……我射獵時，扶我之臂。」向新月呼：「取我舊面，予我新面……救我脫野兔所降之罰。」向星辰：「取我匱乏之心，予爾豐盈之心……取我拙射之臂。」向水蛇：「於沙漠中賜水……聞異族足音，則塞諸泉。」

sensitivity.note: San prayers recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 25 (1919); not verbatim. When the Sun rises after a bitterly cold and hungry night, the father or mother turns the face, with the hands before the eyes, toward the rising Sun, and calls out: 'O Sun, I am so glad to see you perfectly back again, and to take up your work without tiring. Make me just as strong as you, so that when I hunt the game I do not grow tired, hungry and thirsty... Throw toward me that worn-out food which you do not need. Give me of your warmth, that I need not shiver. Hold my arm, when I shoot at game, that my arrow may strike the creature.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 25; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When the Sun goes down and a night of cold and hunger lies before them, they pray again: 'Another day is past, and our stomachs are still hungry, and the cold begins again to gnaw and eat our worn-out bodies. The Lion is ashamed of you, the Leopard fears you, and the Wolf shuns you. If you leave us, they rise from their resting-places to eat us with our wives and children... Come quickly; for without you we do not want to be alone.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 25; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. At new moon they cover their eyes with their hands and cry: 'It is New Moon! Again New Moon! Take my old face from me. Give me your new face... that I may, when I die, come alive again... You said before that we should not die; but should sleep and wake again. But the Hare would not believe and strove with you, and now we are punished for the Hare's sake, to die. Ah, take that punishment from us, that we may only slip into the death-sleep for a while and wake again.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 25; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. To a great bright star: 'Take my heart, which lacks. Give me your heart, which beats in plenty... Take my stomach, which burns with lack. Give me your stomach, filled with the nicest food... Take my arm, which shoots so badly, which cannot hit. Give me your arm, with which you shoot so truly.' And to the Water-Snake: 'Your breast rumbles because it is full of water. The Stars love you — therefore the stone on your head shines. Give us water in the desert... stop up the fountains when you hear the tramp of strangers who come to shoot our game and drive away us and our children.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 25; not verbatim.
